entities.name: Poetic Edda
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Poetic Edda is a medieval Icelandic manuscript containing 31 Old Norse narrative poems in alliterative verse, compiled around the 13th century. This collection of poetry was a cornerstone of Old Norse literature, providing insights into the mythology, legends, and cultural practices of the Viking Age. The Poetic Edda's significance extends beyond its literary value, as it offers a window into the spiritual and cultural beliefs of the Germanic peoples. The manuscript's existence and composition are the result of a complex interplay between the influence of Christianity, the patronage of the Icelandic aristocracy, and the preservation efforts of medieval scribes.

The Poetic Edda's impact can be seen in the subsequent development of Scandinavian literature, folklore, and art. Its influence extends beyond the realm of literature, as it has shaped our understanding of the Viking Age and its cultural heritage. The manuscript's contents, including the famous tale of Sigurd and Fafnir, have been widely studied and adapted in various forms of media.

The Poetic Edda's legacy can be seen in the many translations, adaptations, and reinterpretations of its contents over the centuries. Its influence can be felt in modern literature, art, and popular culture, demonstrating the enduring power of this medieval manuscript.

The Poetic Edda's most striking statistic is the fact that it has survived for over 800 years, a testament to the dedication of medieval scribes and the cultural significance of the Viking Age.

The Poetic Edda's most memorable quote is from the poem 'Völuspá': 'When the mighty god Odin had fallen, / The great wolf Fenrir had broken free, / The earth had shaken, / The sky had been torn apart, / And the fire giant Surtur had emerged from the south.'

The Poetic Edda's lasting cultural footprint can be seen in the numerous films, TV shows, and video games that have adapted its contents, ensuring its continued relevance in modern popular culture.
